system.description:
An evil, malignant creature of tropical jungles. Its true form is a stunted, evil-looking humanoid with bird-like feet and clawed hands, but it can change shape at will into a small wildcat, the form most often seen.

  • Spells: three times a day it can cast curse, omen, divination, fate, ghost light, wind breath, steam breath and transfix; once a day, ancient curse.
  • Claws: it fights with its claws, not very effectively, but any creature it hits must save versus poison or be -1 on all to-hit rolls and saving throws for 2-7 rounds. The effect adds up with each hit.
  • Life tree: its life force is bound to a tree in its forest. If the tree is destroyed, the bajang dies at once, so it goes to great lengths to hide which tree it is.

Bajang usually haunt a small village or settlement, preying on its people at night and trying to take victims in their sleep. Sometimes they serve powerful evil sorcerers as familiars. They are intelligent and very devious, and speak their own language and the local tongue.

OA p.116. Statistics checked against the page images; description rewritten in plain words.

Cousins of the goblin, much like them in nature and habits, except that bakemono come in all shapes and sizes and no two look alike. Skin ranges from brilliant orange and red to deep blue; features may include small stunted wings, hooves, fur, scales, huge noses, feathers, oversized ears and hunched bodies. The DM should let his imagination run.

  • Bands: they gather in bands for raiding and banditry, ruled by an oni or an ogre mage. For every 20 members there is a lieutenant of greater size (HD 2, AC 4, damage 1-8), who takes orders from the oni or ogre mage and rules his 20 absolutely.
  • Lairs: abandoned temples or villages, taken by driving out the rightful owners rather than building their own. Lairs are always in bad repair and look long deserted. 40% of the time they build and man a wooden stockade around it.
  • Arms: they rarely make their own weapons or armor, using what they scavenge and loot: katana 5%; naginata and short sword 20%; spear 40%; tetsubo and short sword 10%; short sword and short bow 10%; chain and shuriken 5%; kusari-gama and trident 10%.
  • In a large force, 20% have armor class 5 from some piece of armor, in poor repair and often badly altered to fit; player characters can't wear it.

Bakemono speak the common tongue, the local human tongue, the oni language and their own (which is like oni). They aren't bright, are easily tricked or outwitted, and have a great weakness for sake and strong drink.

OA p.116. Statistics checked against the page images; description rewritten in plain words.

A lesser spirit bound to a kind of tree, usually one harvested for valuable wood, sap, gum or oil: most often camphor, sometimes teak, mahogany or other valuable woods. Its natural form is a beautiful woman, but it seldom appears so, preferring the form of a small insect.

  • Guardian of trees: a bisan watches over every tree of its kind in its region, and each is bound to one tree; if that tree is damaged or cut down, the bisan suffers the same. It lets people harvest sap, branches, fruit or leaves, and even fell trees at the end of their lives, in exchange for offerings: usually part of each meal and a white cock. Without them it grows angry.
  • Powers: polymorph self, invisibility and becoming ethereal, at will. Once a round it can cast bless (or its reverse), castigate, cause paralysis, pacify, animate wood, wood shape, elemental turning, quickgrowth or ironwood.
  • In a fight: it avoids combat when it can, using spells to cause mischief and hardship. Forced to fight, it flees at the first chance, unless defending its own tree.

Bisan are highly intelligent and clever, and dangerous enemies when angered. Woodsmen usually know where the bisan woods in their area are, and many are marked by local superstition. Bisan speak only their own language.

An overgrown cousin of the common carp, a well-liked food fish. Giant carp live in fresh lakes and rivers of real depth, from cold temperate waters to the tropics. They scavenge, rooting through the bottom ooze, but have been known to rise and attack small boats or swimmers, and some have even taken a baited hook.

  • Swallowing: on a bite that does 12 or more damage, the carp may swallow its victim whole: 8 HD carp swallow creatures the size of a dog, 9 HD a large dog or colt, 10 HD a small man, 11 HD a normal man, 12 HD even a small oni or ogre.
  • A swallowed creature takes the bite's normal damage, then 1 point a round from digestive juices, and has a 5% cumulative chance each round of suffocating.
  • He can be rescued from outside, or cut his way out with an edged weapon; he is free once the carp has lost 50% of its hit points. Those inside fight with no penalty; those outside are -2 to hit (aiming a series of blows at one spot), and thrusting and stabbing weapons have a 20% chance of hitting the victim.

One giant carp can feed a village for some time, so fishermen sometimes organize hunts for them. Such hunts are very dangerous and often cost lives.

An evil spirit; folklore says con-tinh are the spirits of maidens who died before their time. One looks much like a young girl, appears only at night, and is always within 100 feet of an old tree that holds its life force. Damage to the tree damages the con-tinh likewise, and destroying the tree destroys it.

Commoners greatly fear them and shun places where they are said to live, especially at night. By day they hide in the branches of their tree; at night they come out hoping to catch travelers and foolish locals.

  • Laugh: three times a night it can give a weird laugh. Everyone within 20 feet must save versus death or go insane, with intelligence and wisdom reduced to 2 until a heal spell is cast.
  • Possession: once a night it can possess someone, as the spell, and can keep the possession up even by day.
  • It can be hit only by +2 or better weapons. A successful exorcism destroys it.
  • Curse: anyone who destroys a con-tinh's tree must save versus spell or suffer an ancient curse. This happens automatically, day or night.

OA p.118. Statistics checked against the page images; description rewritten in plain words.

The doc cu'o'c looks like half a man standing on one leg, holding the axe it always carries. Given small offerings regularly and included in local worship, it is a kind and helpful spirit that protects the countryside, taking the people of a house or village under its care.

  • It always sees invisible objects and spirits, and can become invisible at will.
  • Spells: once a day each, cure disease, remove paralysis, cure blindness, oath and remove curse; up to three times a day, control weather and becoming astral.
  • Axe: 1d8 damage, plus a huge electric shock doing damage equal to the doc cu'o'c's current hit points (save versus spell for half).
  • It can be hit only by +3 or better weapons.

Its lair is never on the Prime Material Plane but somewhere on the Astral Plane, visited only now and then, where it keeps its offerings and things taken from defeated evil spirits. If the lair is robbed, it returns to the Prime Material Plane, uses its spells to wreak havoc on the land it protected, then leaves and never protects it again.

Doc cu'o'c are great enemies of evil spirits, and most of their protection means driving them off; they also use their spells to bring good weather for crops and harvest. They seldom become directly involved in mortal affairs, at most using spells at night to ease a hardship or right a wrong done to those in their care. A doc cu'o'c protects the land rather than its people, and their good fortune comes mostly as a side effect.

Eastern dragons and the Celestial Bureaucracy. Most eastern dragons are officials of the Celestial Bureaucracy, each kind charged with some part of its government: li lung, the energies of the earth; lung wang, guardians of sea creatures and aides to the Sea Lords; pan lung, guardians of hidden places; shen lung, aides to the chiang lung; t'ien lung, masters of weather (except rain); chiang lung, guardians of rivers and lakes and bringers of rain; tun mi lung, dispensers of ocean storms. (The yu lung holds no office, isn't counted among the greater dragons, and receives no offerings or worship.) Once a year each dragon must go to the Celestial Palace and file a report on the past year; censors examine it and hand out rewards and punishments, and a corrupt or incompetent dragon is often removed and replaced. People learn of a new official, and when he will arrive, through dreams, and prepare a ceremonial procession and a banquet of offerings to win his favor. The other eastern dragons are in the FF.

Chiang lung are the lords of rivers and lakes, answerable to the Celestial Bureaucracy for the creatures of the waters, the giving of rain and the flow of water in their domain. Every river and lake has one, but they seldom show themselves to people outside their domain. They act on the Celestial Emperor's orders and report to him once a year. Though wingless, they fly by the power of a magic pearl in the brain. They speak the languages of the Celestial Court, of fishes and of shen lung, their own, and all human languages.

  • Powers: those common to all eastern dragons, except that they can polymorph into any form. Their breath sends out dark rainclouds, so they can make rain when and where they like, and they can lower water over a 1-square-mile radius per age level. People make offerings asking them to plead with the Celestial Emperor for rain in droughts or less water in floods, but a chiang lung won't act without proper orders, since disobedience is punished by death.
  • At will, once a round: bless, curse, omen, fate, dispel evil, control weather and remove curse. Once a day: major creation and reward. On special orders from the Celestial Emperor they can cast a tsunami.
  • Anyone with a chiang lung can breathe and move underwater as on dry land.
  • Combat: claws and bite. In human form it carries a sword +5 so massive that anyone else needs a successful bend bars/lift gates roll to use it.

Its lair is a magic palace under the water, always huge and rich as befits its rank, however small the river or lake. It is decorated with great wealth and taste, but anything stolen from it becomes worthless on reaching the surface; only gifts freely given are spared. At home the dragon always takes human form (not its true form, but one it seems to prefer), attended by lesser nature spirit servants (also in human form), with 1d6 shen lung as bodyguards and aides, and 2d4 of its children. Away from its lair there is a 75% chance it is with 1d4 lesser nature spirits and a 40% chance with 1-2 shen lung.

Beyond their duties, chiang lung sometimes take part in human affairs. They are especially fond of virtuous scholars and people of learning and art, and sometimes entertain them on richly decorated boats, posing as wealthy nobles or officials; the party lasts all night or until the guest falls asleep, and at dawn he finds himself alone on the boat, often with some token left behind. Their daughters, always strikingly beautiful and gracious, are drawn to handsome men, and secret romances and marriages often follow. A chiang lung often offers a daughter in marriage to a brave or clever hero who visits his court, without the usual formalities of courtship; it is a great honor, and though a man may refuse for noble reasons (a wife at home, or duty to his parents), few do. These matches usually end sadly, as the daughter must at last go home, never to see her husband again. Children of such marriages are spirit folk.

Most eastern dragons are officials of the Celestial Bureaucracy, each kind charged with some part of its government: li lung, the energies of the earth; lung wang, guardians of sea creatures and aides to the Sea Lords; pan lung, guardians of hidden places; shen lung, aides to the chiang lung; t'ien lung, masters of weather (except rain); chiang lung, guardians of rivers and lakes and bringers of rain; tun mi lung, dispensers of ocean storms. A fearsome dragon of the seas and oceans, most often met in the sky along coasts or far out to sea. It is wingless, flying by the power of a magic pearl in its brain. The Celestial Emperor has charged it with raising the destructive typhoons and hurricanes that ravage warmer coasts, a task it greatly enjoys. It is supposed to act only on the Bureaucracy's orders, but often forgets and goes on destructive rampages out of pure malice, and it is so powerful that even the Celestial Emperor finds it hard to restrain and punish.

  • Typhoon: besides the usual powers of an eastern dragon, it can summon a divine wind (as the spell) of great strength, with a radius in miles of five times its age level. It can do this once a week; the storm lasts 6d4 hours, with the dragon always at its center, moving with it as it travels.
  • Combat: if the storm isn't enough, it fights with claws and bite. It has no breath weapon.
  • It is immune to all water- and air-based attacks.

Nothing certain is known of their lairs. As members of the Celestial Bureaucracy they probably keep palaces under the sea suited to their rank, likely in remote corners of the ocean, since their evil nature makes them unwelcome among more peaceful, cultured sea creatures. They speak the languages of all sea creatures, the Celestial Court and the Sea Lords.

An intelligent shapechanging animal, like a hengeyokai, but with only two forms: a particularly foul, ugly giant rat, or a ratman. It has its full hit points and abilities in either.

  • Rat form: it bites, and each hit has a 5% chance of passing on a disease, most often cholera, plague or fevers.
  • Ratman form: it fights with weapons and can wear armor, preferring spears, naginatas and two-handed swords.
  • King: when 10 or more are met, one is the group's "king", with 5 HD, AC 4, and +2 damage on its bite.
  • Fear of cats: faced with any feline creature, a goblin rat saves versus paralyzation or flees in panic. Cat-like creatures are +1 to hit against goblin rats, from the hatred between them and the rats' superstitious fear. Even a lifelike painting of a cat protects a household; a painting of quality made for this purpose counts.

Goblin rats live at the edges of human settlements, stealing food and livestock and now and then preying on lone travelers. They lair in a deserted temple or an abandoned hut in the forest, its people slain or driven off. They have no language of their own but speak the common tongue and the local human tongue.

system.description:
The goblin spider, or earth spider, looks like a huge, furry spider of especially evil cast. They live far from people in rough wooded mountains. They once ruled much of the land people now hold, and see humans and their allies as invaders of their homeland, so they take every chance to harm travelers and settlers at the edges of their territory.

  • Ambush: they spin no webs but live in underground tunnels with carefully hidden trapdoor entrances. They sense the vibrations of creatures passing overhead and spring out suddenly, surprising on 1-4.
  • Grasp: in combat they try to grab a victim, drag him into the lair and shut the door. In any round a goblin spider hits with both attacks, the victim is grasped and held, fighting at -4 to hit. He can break free with a successful bend bars/lift gates roll; others can pull him loose with a combined strength of 20 or more (at least two characters). While holding a victim, the spider can make no other attacks.
  • Mimicry: they can imitate any voice or animal sound they hear, though in languages they don't know they can only repeat words they have heard. Not very intelligent, but clever and devious, they often use mimicry to lure victims to their deaths.
  • 30% chance 2d4 giant spiders live near the lair, serving as guards and helping in any fight.

They speak their own language, the language of spiders, the common tongue and the tongue of the humans near their lair.

system.description:
An aquatic people: humanoids with webbed hands and feet and soft fur that shimmers in many colors. They live in the warm shallow seas of sub-tropical and tropical waters, fishing and attending the court of the Lord of the Sea. They speak only their own language and the court language of the Sea Lord.

  • Communities: simple: sunken ship hulls and thick kelp beds meet their needs. They love bright treasures and collect precious cargoes from wrecks. Their society is ruled by females, and 75% of those met are female. Each community is led by a matron with 6 HD and AC 5, and 2d6 tamed sharks defend it. They are on good terms with sharks, porpoises and whales: 40% chance 3d4 of these are with any band.
  • Arms: short sword 20%; trident and speargun (treat as spear) 50%; trident and dagger 20%; short sword and net 10%.
  • Temper: peaceful and friendly, they seldom attack ships and much prefer to be left alone, but they defend their hunting grounds and homes fiercely. Fishermen in their waters often find lines cut, nets fouled and small leaks in their hulls; if that doesn't discourage them, the hai nu ask the Lord of the Sea for stronger action.
  • They can't survive long out of water, taking 1 point of damage each round wholly out of it. They take double damage from fire attacks and +1 per die from cold attacks, and are immune to all water-based attacks.

OA p.122. Statistics checked against the page images; description rewritten in plain words.

A race of ape-like humanoids with white fur and the faces of men, living in mountainous sub-tropical forests. They speak their own language and the common tongue.

  • Trade: they usually want to be left alone, but a weakness for strong drink brings them now and then to human villages to trade. They bring rare treasures from their hidden forest homes (parrots, feathers of rare birds, scented woods, exotic fruits) for forged metal, pottery, wine and rice. They practice no crafts, preferring a simple life, and some scholars hold them up as perfect examples of harmony with nature and non-action.
  • War season: once a year they become extremely savage and aggressive, forming raiding bands that attack settlements at the edge of their land, good and evil alike. They are clever enough never to strike the same place two years running. They carry spears, parangs, blowguns and wicker shields.
  • Poisons: they are skilled with poison and always dip their blowgun darts. One poison kills on a failed save versus poison, or does 1d8 damage on a successful one. The other is a strong muscle relaxant that paralyzes for 2d6 turns on a failed save, and slows the victim for 1d6 turns on a successful one.
  • Lair: a large forest tree with simple thatched sleeping platforms in its branches, holding females and children equal to 50% of the number met. The females have 1 hit die and fight from the branches, throwing clubs and stones at attackers.

Hsing-sing despise the tasloi, which sometimes wander up from their tropical homes on raids.

OA p.122. Statistics checked against the page images; description rewritten in plain words.

A race of shapeshifting foxes of supernatural origin, in many ways like hengeyokai. A hu hsien has two forms: a fox that can walk on its hind legs and hold things in its front paws, and a human maiden of exceptional beauty and grace (charisma 18). It can be recognized because its tail never changes, though it cleverly hides it under its robes.

  • At will, one a round: invisibility, polymorph self, disguise, chameleon, know history, hypnotism, read magic, comprehend languages, ventriloquism, apparition, ESP and hypnotic pattern.
  • Once a day: possess, servant horde and major creation. Three times a week: reward or ancient curse.
  • Fascination: in human form, it has the power of fascination.
  • Hit only by +3 or better weapons. It regenerates 2 hit points an hour. Immune to fire; half damage from cold (none on a successful save); double damage from electricity. It greatly fears thunderstorms, since the Celestial Emperor sometimes sends the Thunder God to punish hu hsien for their wickedness.

Life force: hu hsien live, and gain their shapeshifting power, by draining the life force of humans. In human form, one snares a victim, usually with fascination so that he falls hopelessly in love with it. Each day he then spends with it costs him one level of experience. Blinded by love, he doesn't know what is happening or realize he has been harmed. Once it starts, he can be saved only if others drive away or destroy the hu hsien.

They aren't wholly cruel or ungrateful: they have rewarded or helped people who helped them or showed them kindness and generosity, usually with success at the examinations, good fortune, or rescue from great danger. They are especially drawn to scholars, for good and ill, and are known for devious tricks, especially on those who scoff at their existence. They are very fond of wine and can't resist it, but once drunk they change back to their true form against their will.

They usually lair at the edge of a human village, sometimes in an abandoned house made by illusion to look rich and luxurious, sometimes in a fox den enchanted to look like a great mansion inside. Many an unlucky traveler has dined and slept in a grand hall, only to wake in the cramped space under the floor of an old house.

system.description:
A most unusual spirit, very hard to detect or destroy: a projection of the evil thoughts of a living person. It comes into being from intense hatred or jealousy, without that person knowing, and once it exists it has a will of its own, seeking to harm the object of that anger or jealousy. It has no form or real body, only a presence of psychic energy.

  • Detecting it: it can't be seen or detected with detect invisibility or detect life. Detect evil shows an aura of evil around the victim; detect harmony shows something about the victim and his surroundings is out of balance; true sight shows the ikiryo, appearing to the caster as the person it sprang from.
  • Against it: protection from spirits or protection from evil 10' radius keeps it out but doesn't harm it. Invisibility to spirits keeps it from finding its victim. Dispel evil drives it away for 24 hours. Summon spirit makes it take the form of its source. A successful exorcism banishes it forever. If the person it came from is confronted with its existence, it vanishes forever.
  • Draining: it finds its victim and stays with him until destroyed. For each 24 hours it stays, he loses 1 point from every ability score, feeling disturbed and restless, the air heavy and stale, and growing tired and worn out. If any score reaches 0, he dies. Lost points return only when the ikiryo is destroyed, at 1 point per ability a day.

Using it: the DM can have an ikiryo attack a player character, or spring from one. If a non-player character secretly resents a player character, the ikiryo attacks that player character; if a player character holds a grudge against a non-player character, the ikiryo attacks that non-player character, and once found and traced back, causes the player character trouble. A character can never consciously call up an ikiryo, and it never acts for his good.

The earthquake beetle, a giant beetle of shimmering blue-green with a hard shell hiding small wings. It prowls temperate forests for meat, its main food, and is especially drawn to the smell of oxen, sometimes attacking them as they work in the fields.

  • Mandibles: it grabs victims and drags them back into the trees, but its mandibles are badly made for clamping, so a character can easily slip free.
  • Tremors: more dangerous are the throbbing tremors it makes by striking its abdomen on the ground, weak at first and growing with each blow:
    • Round 1: everyone within 5 feet saves versus breath weapon or is knocked down.
    • Round 2: the same, within 10 feet.
    • Round 3: within 15 feet; those within 5 feet are thrown violently about, take 1d6 damage and lose their attack that round.
    • Round 4: within 20 feet; those within 10 feet take the damage.
    • Round 5: 25 feet and 15 feet. Cracks open in the ground within 5 feet.
    • Round 6: 30 feet and 20 feet, and everything within 10 feet suffers an earthquake spell. The beetle then takes to the air to escape the results of its own work.

Incense makers prize its ichor, paying as much as 1 gp a flask.

system.description:
A spirit of the dead in the form of a demon-ghost, which can happen when someone dies unburied, with his life's work unfinished, or by unavenged violence. It looks exactly as the person did in life, with a solid-seeming body, but can't be touched: things pass harmlessly through it. Sunlight doesn't affect it, but it is most active at night. Its alignment depends on the task it must fulfill.

Hit diceWeapon needed to hitDamage
3+11-6
4+21-8
5+31-10
6+41-12
  • It can become ethereal at will, and possess a person, as the spell, three times a day.
  • Immune to ESP and all charm, enchantment, illusion and water spells, and to all psionic attacks. Normal fire and cold don't harm it; magical fire and cold do half damage.

When met, a kuei usually tries to possess a victim. If it succeeds, its own form vanishes and it uses the victim's body to finish whatever task still binds it to the Prime Material Plane: avenging itself on its killer, fulfilling an oath, or arranging the temple ceremonies needed to release it. Fulfilling an oath, it may keep the victim for a long time; one story tells of a kuei that possessed her sister to keep a promise of marriage, living with the promised husband for many years before being found out. The possession ends only with the victim's death, the task's completion, or exorcism (or another spell for driving out spirits). Then the victim returns to his senses, knowing nothing of what happened.

system.description:
Like buccaneers and pirates elsewhere, the wako sail the warm seas, boarding ships and raiding coastal towns, a vicious scourge feared by everyone who travels the warm seas. They are lowborn men who fled their homelands or were hired by powerful lords, desperate and dangerous; even other pirates who have met them fear them.

  • Ferocity: they have no fear of death. Knowing horrible torture and death await them if captured, they fight to the last man however hopeless it is, and take no prisoners except women, carried off as slaves. All wako fight at +2 to hit and +1 damage.
  • Leaders: for every 30 wako there is a 5th level bushi, and for every 60 a 7th level barbarian, in addition to the number rolled. They are always led by a 10th level samurai, with a barbarian lieutenant of 8th level and 1-3 bushi mates of 6th level. For every 30 wako there is a 5% chance of a wu jen of 6th to 9th level.
  • Arms and armor: hara-ate-gawa and sword 50%; sword and bow 10%; do-maru and sword 15%; kote and spear 10%; kote, do-maru, sword and bow 5%; haramaki, sword, spear and bow 10%. All leaders and high-level wako wear o-yoroi.
  • Lair: a permanent settlement, perhaps on their sponsoring lord's lands, walled, well defended and patrolled.

system.description:
A close relative of mermen and mermaids, almost identical to them except for flaming red hair. Ningyo live under the waves and rarely come up, preferring to serve the Sea Lord than to meddle in the affairs of men, but they are quite kind and helpful to people. Sailors think of them as protectors and sometimes make offerings to them, especially in great storms.

  • They usually carry no weapons; when armed, they carry a trident or spear. They are peaceful and avoid fights when they can, but if forced, fight with whatever weapons are at hand.
  • Spells: they cast spells as a shukenja and a wu jen of a level equal to their hit dice: a 3 HD ningyo casts as a 3rd level shukenja and wu jen.
  • They form no communities, roaming with the currents and the schools of fish they feed on.
  • They can't survive long out of water, losing 1 hit point each round above the surface.

They speak the languages of the Sea Lord and of fishes, and the common tongue.

OA p.126. Statistics checked against the page images; description rewritten in plain words.

A small humanoid two to three feet tall, with ruddy bronze skin and red hair: a wandering spirit, active by day and night. Common folk greatly fear it for its powers and often give it gifts and offerings to keep it content. It is usually found in farmland well away from towns.

  • Drying touch: it attacks with a club cut from a withered, dead tree or with an iron rod. Besides the damage, anyone struck saves versus spell; on a failure the drying touch dries him out, costing 1 point of constitution. At constitution 2 he can't fight or stand; at 0 he dies.
  • It can become invisible at will.
  • Drought: more feared is its power to create drought (as the wu jen spell) once a week, over an area 5 miles across, lasting until the p'oh ends it, is slain, or the spell is countered (by ice blight).

A p'oh usually arrives somewhere, finds a safe lair, then shows itself to the peasants, announcing that it has settled there and that they must honor and appease it, or else. As long as they leave suitable offerings (which it collects while invisible), it stays and makes no mischief. If the offerings are too little, refused or missed, it grows angry and brings drought. So small shrines to the p'oh are often seen along country roads. Now and then the Celestial Emperor sends one to punish an area's people for some failing or crime. It speaks its own language and the common tongue.

system.description:
A race of foot-tall humanoids in wooded hills, known for being fearless and private, with little to do with the outside world. They are quick to take offense, equally quick to return it, and very good at defending themselves.

  • Bird form: they can polymorph three times a day into a bird (hence their flying speed).
  • They fight with short swords, darts and uchi-ne.
  • Disease: once a day they can cause disease, as the spell, without touching the victim; they only point at him within 10 feet.

Gargantua are truly monstrous in size and ferocity, towering over almost anything they meet. The most common are giant humanoids, insects and reptiles. Whether they are freaks of nature, throwbacks to an age when they ruled the land, or the results of mad magical experiments is unknown; all that is known is that they exist and now and then appear to ravage the land. They have some intelligence, but mostly act like mindless brutes bent on destruction for its own sake.

  • The ground shakes as they walk, so they can never surprise anyone; their height makes them easy to see from afar, and they squeal and roar as they move and fight, so their presence is almost impossible to miss.
  • All regenerate 4 hit points a round.

Fortunately they are rare and seldom trouble people. When one does appear, it is treated as a national (or at least regional) emergency, and every resource is used to get rid of it.

Humanoid gargantua are the least intelligent kind: 80 to 100 feet tall, sometimes furry. They have no language, but 25% of the time they grasp the meaning of other languages through a strong empathy for human feelings. They strike with two fists for 4d10 each, and can trample anyone underfoot for 10-100 damage. They live on jagged, remote mountains or tiny islands far out at sea.

The Animal Kings send their three main generals, General Tiger, General Ox and General Monkey, on their errands. In natural form each looks like a giant-sized humanoid version of his animal, dressed in the armor, robes and weapons of a lord of the Animal Kings' court.

General Tiger is extremely proud, hot-tempered and bloodthirsty.

Kappa are small amphibious humanoids of lakes, ponds, rivers and streams, about two feet tall and shaped like a young boy, with a thick tortoise-like shell on the back (AC -2 against attacks from behind). The top of the head is hollow, a small bowl filled with water.

  • Strength: all kappa have exceptional strength (18/00): +3 to hit and the listed damage.
  • Martial arts: each masters one martial arts style, including 1d6 of its special maneuvers. In combat they fight with clawed hands, rending their foes.
  • All kappa regenerate 1 hit point a round.
  • The bowl: their power comes from water: the bowl on the head is filled from the stream or lake where they live, and as long as it stays full they keep their powers. If it is ever emptied, the kappa loses its powers: its strength becomes normal, it can't regenerate, and it loses 2 hit points a round until the water is restored. A few can sometimes be tricked into bowing (and so spilling the water), but most are too clever. In combat, a foe can spill it with a successful bend bars/lift gates roll, made for this purpose or for a martial arts throw maneuver; otherwise the kappa's natural agility and grace keep it from spilling.
  • Kappa are immune to water-based spells.

Kappa live in fresh water, lairing under rocks and bridges. They usually appear to waylay lone travelers and drag them underwater to their doom, and are especially fond of horseflesh, often trying to grab horses and drag them under. They are said to love melons and cucumbers and to be appeased by offerings of them; where kappa are known to live, people often throw a few into the water before crossing a bridge or straying near the bank, hoping the kappa will leave them alone.

system.description:
Nature spirits are the outward signs of the powers in plants and natural things. Lesser nature spirits belong to trees, flowers, rocks and bamboo groves; greater ones to mountains, boulders, plains, very ancient trees and small islands. Each is tied to one thing or place that holds its life force, and what happens to that thing happens to the spirit: cutting down a lesser spirit's tree kills it, and an earthquake on a greater spirit's mountain may anger or hurt it, depending on the damage.

  • Two aspects: every nature spirit has a good aspect (gentle, helpful, kind) and an evil one (malicious, savage, cruel). When met, there is a 75% chance the good aspect rules.
  • They usually shun the mortal world, living quietly in and throughout the thing that holds their life force, but show themselves in times of danger, and often to meet or test people of renown.
  • All nature spirits, at will, once a round: invisibility, polymorph self, detect evil (and good), detect magic and detect harmony.

Lesser nature spirits are usually met near their life source, most often polymorphed into a handsome man or beautiful maiden (charisma 19). They know everything about the area around their life source, so they can find hidden treasures and lost things there easily. They have no other special powers. A lesser nature spirit often falls in love with and marries a mortal, the stuff of many tales and legends.

Nature spirits are the outward signs of the powers in plants and natural things. Lesser nature spirits belong to trees, flowers, rocks and bamboo groves; greater ones to mountains, boulders, plains, very ancient trees and small islands. Each is tied to one thing or place that holds its life force, and what happens to that thing happens to the spirit: cutting down a lesser spirit's tree kills it, and an earthquake on a greater spirit's mountain may anger or hurt it, depending on the damage.

  • Two aspects: every nature spirit has a good aspect (gentle, helpful, kind) and an evil one (malicious, savage, cruel). When met, there is a 75% chance the good aspect rules.
  • They usually shun the mortal world, living quietly in and throughout the thing that holds their life force, but show themselves in times of danger, and often to meet or test people of renown.
  • All nature spirits, at will, once a round: invisibility, polymorph self, detect evil (and good), detect magic and detect harmony.

Greater nature spirits are far more powerful.

  • Shapechange five times a day; know history and aura at will; reward once a week; ancient curse once a week.
  • Once a day each, they can cast every wu jen spell of the element of their life source (except conjure elemental): a greater mountain spirit all earth spells; a greater island spirit all water spells (the water being stronger than the land here).
  • Hit only by +4 or better weapons, and immune to magical attacks that use their own element.
  • Like the lesser spirits, they know everything that happens in the area of their life source.

Unlike lesser spirits, they tend to be aloof, haughty and irritable. If a village is built on the slope of a greater mountain spirit, he may take offense and try to drive the settlers off. People take great care not to upset them, making offerings and consulting shukenja before any undertaking that might disturb one. They seldom marry humans.

Oni are fearsome spirits of desolate, forbidding places. Common oni stand seven to eight feet tall, with one to three eyes and one or two horns. Their arms and legs are covered with coarse hair, and their hands end in dirty, thick talons. Their skin is usually red, but green, black, orange and purple ones have been seen; blue-skinned oni also exist, better known as ogre magi. They dress like the local people, but their clothes and gear are more ragged and dirty.

Common oni live in rocky mountains, deserted ruins, graveyards and other places commonly thought haunted. Sometimes one settles at a shrine or gate along a lonely road and terrorizes everyone who passes. They are bloodthirsty and cruel, attacking for food and for the sheer joy of cruelty.

  • They usually fight with two-handed swords (in one hand) or their powerful claws.
  • Powers: polymorph self three times a day; fly (as the spell) three times a day; invisibility twice a day; cloud trapeze (for themselves only) once a day; cause fear at will.
  • Followers: they often command lesser creatures such as bakemono, goblin rats and gaki. When met, 10% chance of 2d10 such followers; in their lair there are always 4d10 bakemono or goblin rats, attending the court of the more powerful oni.

They speak their own language and those of tengu, bakemono and hengeyokai, and the local human tongue.

Go-zu oni stand eight to nine feet tall, with hulking bodies and the heads of bulls. Unlike common oni, they are servants and soldiers of the Celestial Emperor: with the me-zu oni they form the bulk of his army in times of trouble and rebellion. They also oversee the lands of the dead and escort the unwilling departed there. They wear armor and robes suited to their rank as the Celestial Emperor's soldiers.

  • They fight with two-handed swords, spears, naginatas, halberds and tridents, making two attacks a round with a weapon or their hands, and goring with their horns.
  • Powers: polymorph self, cause fear, invisibility, fly and fire shuriken at will; cloud trapeze twice a day. They automatically detect invisible creatures and objects.
  • They regenerate 3 hit points a round and have the strength of a hill giant.

They speak all human languages and those of tengu, oni, bakemono, animals and the Celestial Court.

  • Besides the go-zu's weapons, they use whips and lassos to deal with their victims.
  • Powers: polymorph self, invisibility, cause fear and fly at will; become ethereal or astral twice a day; cloud trapeze three times a day.
  • They cast spells as a wu jen of a level equal to their hit dice, and always see as with true seeing.
  • They regenerate 3 hit points a round and have the strength of a stone giant.

system.description:
Tengu are bird-like humanoids of empty mountain country not far from settled lands. Many believe they were the land's first inhabitants before humans came; with the arrival of humans and their organization and culture, the tengu were pushed deeper into the mountains, where they now live in forest glades, meadows and beside streams and ponds. They are rather solitary and form no villages or permanent communities.

All tengu are extremely secretive and capricious, and little is known of their way of life. They are all very fond of strong drink and can be bribed, appeased or befriended with large offerings of sake. They also love music, especially flute and drum.

Crow-headed tengu are humanoids two to three feet tall with the head and beak of a crow and feathered wings between the shoulder blades. They are evil and malicious, seeking to harm any human who strays into their land. They fight with katana and wakizashi, speak their own language, that of animals and the local human tongue, and can perfectly mimic voices they have heard. Three times a day they can use polymorph self and shout. They rank below humanoid tengu and obey them out of respect for rank.

Tengu are bird-like humanoids of empty mountain country not far from settled lands. Many believe they were the land's first inhabitants before humans came; with the arrival of humans and their organization and culture, the tengu were pushed deeper into the mountains, where they now live in forest glades, meadows and beside streams and ponds. They are rather solitary and form no villages or permanent communities.

All tengu are extremely secretive and capricious, and little is known of their way of life. They are all very fond of strong drink and can be bribed, appeased or befriended with large offerings of sake. They also love music, especially flute and drum.

Humanoid tengu stand three to four feet tall, with human faces except for red or blue skin and very long noses. Some have stunted feathered wings between the shoulder blades.

  • Powers: polymorph self, shout and phantasmal force three times a day; invisibility at will; reward or ancient curse once a week; misdirection once a turn; ghost light once a round. They can mimic any human or animal sound perfectly.
  • They cast spells as a shukenja and fight as a kensai, each of a level equal to their hit dice, and know one martial arts style with 2-5 of its special maneuvers.
  • Feather fan: each carries a fan of brightly colored feathers. Folded, it works as a normal katana. Fanned, it raises a wind like a strong gale (as wind breath), casts quickgrowth, or makes a facial feature grow or shrink abnormally (most often the nose or ears).

Not evil, but not fond of humans, humanoid tengu often play cruel tricks on them. They like shukenja, wu jen and kensai who specialize in the sword, and now and then tutor a sword kensai in the secrets of their skill; such tutoring takes 1 to 3 months and automatically earns the kensai 1,000 experience points.

They speak their own language, the local human tongue and the languages of animals.
